question: A recent American study shows that nine out of ten students feel compelled to express more progressive views than those they actually hold1. They are thus attempting to escape pressure from lecturers and students with left-wing leanings, which can result in biased grading, harassment, or even violence.

This has also given rise in a dramatic decline in the standards and rankings of the schools and universities most affected by the militant monopoly of the left and far left, which apply the theory of social engineering by making it too costly to express dissenting opinions.
The peddlers of these ideologies, who are over-represented in academia, claim however that academic freedom is threatened by any criticism of their views. 1.
At a time when European institutions are issuing numerous communications and standards on academic freedom, can the Commission provide a precise legal definition of it?
Does this encompass only so-called progressive views, as left-wing academics and student activists claim?
Will the Commission undertake to strip universities that support the most violent far-left activists, particularly when they threaten dissident teachers or students of EU funding?
Supporter2
answer: The Commission participates actively to the European Higher Education Area as a full member of the Bologna Follow-Up Group (1). The Rome Communiqué (2) defined academic freedom in 2020 as freedom of academic staff and students to engage in research, teaching, learning and communication in and with society without interference nor fear of reprisal.

The Tirana Communiqué (2024) reaffirmed that academic freedom is one of six fundamental academic values, next to academic integrity, institutional autonomy, student and staff participation in higher education governance, public responsibility for higher education and public responsibility of higher education, and that these values must be implemented as a coherent whole.

Enshrined in Article 13 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights (3), academic freedom guarantees academics and students the freedom of thought and inquiry needed to advance knowledge through research and exchange openly. It is informed by the standards of academic disciplines and provides the condition for challenging these standards based on the results of research.

Therefore, these fundamental values should be understood as foundational principles of higher education rather than as political positions. Education is a national competence. The Commission has therefore limited direct ascendancy over higher education institutions.

However, regulatory requirements of EU programmes such as Erasmus+ and Horizon Europe (4) attach conditions and create incentives that support respect for these principles as part of eligibility for funding.
